topic.subject: Chemistry
topic.title: Ions in Aqueous Solution and Inorganic Tests

questions.q: Sodium hydroxide solution is added to a solution containing \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}(aq)}\) ions. What is seen?
questions.solution: \(\mathrm{[Fe(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+} + 2OH^{-} \rightarrow [Fe(H_{2}O)_{4}(OH)_{2}] + 2H_{2}O}\): a green precipitate of iron(II) hydroxide, which does not dissolve in excess. (Orange-brown is iron(III) hydroxide; the green precipitate slowly turns brown at its surface as air oxidises it.)

questions.q: Which is the formula of the precipitate formed when sodium hydroxide solution is added to \(\mathrm{[Fe(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{3+}(aq)}\)?
questions.solution: Three hydroxide ions each remove a proton from a water ligand, giving the neutral complex: \(\mathrm{[Fe(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{3+} + 3OH^{-} \rightarrow [Fe(H_{2}O)_{3}(OH)_{3}] + 3H_{2}O}\). A neutral complex is insoluble, so it precipitates. (Charged complexes stay in solution.)

questions.q: Which statement best explains why a solution of \(\mathrm{[Fe(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{3+}}\) ions is more acidic than a solution of \(\mathrm{[Fe(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}}\) ions of the same concentration?

options.A: \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\) has a higher charge/size ratio, so it polarises the water ligands more and weakens their O–H bonds, releasing \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) more readily.
options.B: \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\) is a larger ion, so it holds the water ligands less tightly and they are released as \(\mathrm{H_{3}O^{+}}\).
options.C: \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\) has more d electrons, which repel the hydrogen atoms of the water ligands.
options.D: \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\) forms more co-ordinate bonds, so there are more water ligands to lose protons.

questions.solution: \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\) has a higher charge and a smaller radius than \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\). It attracts electron density from the oxygen of each water ligand more strongly, weakening the O–H bonds, so protons are released more easily: \(\mathrm{[Fe(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{3+} + H_{2}O \rightleftharpoons [Fe(H_{2}O)_{5}(OH)]^{2+} + H_{3}O^{+}}\). (Both ions are six-co-ordinate; \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\) has fewer d electrons, not more.)

questions.q: Which equation shows why an aqueous solution of aluminium ions is acidic?
questions.solution: The hexaaqua ion acts as a Brønsted–Lowry acid: one water ligand gives a proton to a solvent water molecule, forming \(\mathrm{H_{3}O^{+}}\): \(\mathrm{[Al(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{3+} + H_{2}O \rightleftharpoons [Al(H_{2}O)_{5}(OH)]^{2+} + H_{3}O^{+}}\). The other equations release no \(\mathrm{H_{3}O^{+}}\), so they cannot explain the acidity.

questions.q: Ammonia solution is added dropwise to a solution containing \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}(aq)}\) ions until it is in excess. What is seen?

options.A: A pale blue precipitate forms, which does not dissolve in excess.
options.B: A green precipitate forms, which dissolves in excess to give a dark green solution.
options.C: No precipitate forms; the solution turns deep blue at once.
options.D: A pale blue precipitate forms, which dissolves in excess to give a deep blue solution.

questions.solution: A little ammonia acts as a base, giving blue \(\mathrm{[Cu(H_{2}O)_{4}(OH)_{2}]}\). In excess, ammonia acts as a ligand and the precipitate dissolves by ligand exchange, forming deep blue \(\mathrm{[Cu(NH_{3})_{4}(H_{2}O)_{2}]^{2+}}\). (With excess sodium hydroxide the blue precipitate stays.)

questions.q: Which equation shows copper(II) hydroxide dissolving in excess ammonia solution?
questions.solution: This is ligand exchange, and it is incomplete: four ammonia ligands replace the two hydroxide and two of the water ligands, leaving \(\mathrm{[Cu(NH_{3})_{4}(H_{2}O)_{2}]^{2+}}\), with two water molecules and two hydroxide ions released. (Copper(II) hydroxide is not amphoteric, so it does not form \(\mathrm{[Cu(OH)_{4}]^{2-}}\); and a neutral product would not dissolve.)

questions.q: Which metal hydroxide precipitate dissolves when excess sodium hydroxide solution is added?
questions.solution: Aluminium hydroxide is amphoteric: it reacts with acids and with bases. In excess hydroxide it loses another proton to form a soluble, colourless complex ion: \(\mathrm{[Al(H_{2}O)_{3}(OH)_{3}] + OH^{-} \rightarrow [Al(H_{2}O)_{2}(OH)_{4}]^{-} + H_{2}O}\). The iron and copper hydroxides do not dissolve in excess sodium hydroxide.

questions.q: Excess ammonia solution is added to the grey-green precipitate of chromium(III) hydroxide, and the precipitate dissolves. Which complex forms, and what type of reaction is this?
questions.solution: In excess ammonia the ammonia molecules replace the ligands: \(\mathrm{[Cr(H_{2}O)_{3}(OH)_{3}] + 6NH_{3} \rightarrow [Cr(NH_{3})_{6}]^{3+} + 3H_{2}O + 3OH^{-}}\), giving a purple solution. This is ligand exchange. (\(\mathrm{[Cr(OH)_{6}]^{3-}}\) forms with excess sodium hydroxide, by amphoteric behaviour: protons are removed, no ligand is swapped.)

questions.q: Ammonia solution is added dropwise to a solution containing \(\mathrm{Co^{2+}(aq)}\) ions until it is in excess. What is seen?

options.A: A blue precipitate forms, which dissolves in excess to give a straw-coloured solution.
options.B: A blue precipitate forms, which does not dissolve in excess.
options.C: A pink precipitate forms, which dissolves in excess to give a blue solution.
options.D: A green precipitate forms, which dissolves in excess to give a deep blue solution.

questions.solution: A little ammonia gives blue \(\mathrm{[Co(H_{2}O)_{4}(OH)_{2}]}\). Excess ammonia exchanges the ligands, forming straw-coloured (pale yellow-brown) \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_{3})_{6}]^{2+}}\), which slowly darkens in air as cobalt(II) is oxidised to cobalt(III). (With excess sodium hydroxide the precipitate stays.)

questions.q: Sodium carbonate solution is added to a solution containing \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}(aq)}\) ions. What is seen?

options.A: An orange-brown precipitate and no effervescence
options.B: A green precipitate and no effervescence

questions.solution: \(\mathrm{[Fe(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{3+}}\) is acidic enough to react with carbonate ions, giving carbon dioxide (effervescence) and a precipitate of iron(III) hydroxide, \(\mathrm{[Fe(H_{2}O)_{3}(OH)_{3}]}\). (A green precipitate without bubbles is iron(II) carbonate, from \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\).)

questions.q: Sodium carbonate solution gives a precipitate of \(\mathrm{FeCO_{3}}\) with \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}(aq)}\), but a precipitate of iron(III) hydroxide with \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}(aq)}\). Which statement best explains the difference?

options.A: Iron(III) carbonate is soluble in water, so it does not precipitate.
options.B: \(\mathrm{[Fe(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{3+}}\) is a stronger acid, so it protonates the carbonate ions, releasing carbon dioxide.
options.C: \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\) oxidises the carbonate ions to carbon dioxide.
options.D: Carbonate ions act as ligands towards \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\), forming a soluble complex instead.

questions.solution: The higher charge/size ratio of \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\) makes its hexaaqua ion acidic enough to give protons to carbonate ions, so \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\) is released and the hydroxide precipitates. \(\mathrm{[Fe(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}}\) is too weak an acid, so the carbonate simply precipitates. (Carbon is +4 in both carbonate and \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\), so no oxidation occurs.)

questions.q: Excess sodium carbonate solution is added to 25.0 \(\text{cm}^{3}\) of \(0.200\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\) iron(III) chloride. What volume of carbon dioxide forms, measured at room temperature and pressure? (Molar gas volume = \(24.0\ \text{dm}^{3}\ \text{mol}^{-1}\))

A colourless solution gives a white precipitate with sodium hydroxide solution, which dissolves in excess. With sodium carbonate solution it gives a white precipitate and effervescence. Which ion is present?
questions.solution: Only aluminium hydroxide is amphoteric, so only it dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide. The effervescence with carbonate shows an acidic 3+ aqua ion. (\(\mathrm{Mg(OH)_{2}}\) does not dissolve in excess; \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) gives green precipitates.)

questions.q: A small amount of ammonia solution gives the same precipitate with \(\mathrm{[Fe(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}}\) as sodium hydroxide does. Why?

options.A: Ammonia acts as a Brønsted–Lowry base, removing protons from two of the water ligands.
options.B: Ammonia acts as a ligand, replacing two of the water ligands.
options.C: Ammonia reduces the \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) ion, which then precipitates.
options.D: Ammonia makes the solution acidic, which lowers the solubility of the complex.

questions.solution: \(\mathrm{[Fe(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+} + 2NH_{3} \rightarrow [Fe(H_{2}O)_{4}(OH)_{2}] + 2NH_{4}^{+}}\). The ammonia accepts protons, so it is acting as a base, not a ligand, and the same neutral hydroxide precipitates as with \(\mathrm{OH^{-}}\) ions.

questions.q: Which test shows that a solid contains ammonium ions, \(\mathrm{NH_{4}^{+}}\)?

options.A: Warm it with sodium hydroxide solution; the gas given off turns damp blue litmus paper red.
options.B: Add dilute hydrochloric acid; the gas given off turns limewater milky.
options.C: Dissolve it and add acidified silver nitrate; a white precipitate forms.
options.D: Warm it with sodium hydroxide solution; the gas given off turns damp red litmus paper blue.

questions.solution: \(\mathrm{NH_{4}^{+} + OH^{-} \rightarrow NH_{3} + H_{2}O}\). Ammonia is the only common alkaline gas, so it turns damp red litmus blue. The paper must be damp so that the ammonia can dissolve and form hydroxide ions.

questions.q: Both solid sodium carbonate and solid sodium hydrogencarbonate fizz with dilute acid. How can they be told apart?

options.A: Add dilute hydrochloric acid: only sodium carbonate gives off carbon dioxide.
options.B: Do a flame test: only sodium hydrogencarbonate gives a yellow-orange flame.
options.C: Heat each solid: only sodium hydrogencarbonate gives off a gas that turns limewater milky.
options.D: Heat each solid: only sodium carbonate gives off a gas that turns limewater milky.

questions.solution: Sodium hydrogencarbonate decomposes on heating: \(\mathrm{2NaHCO_{3} \rightarrow Na_{2}CO_{3} + H_{2}O + CO_{2}}\). Sodium carbonate, a Group 1 carbonate, is stable at Bunsen temperatures. Both give \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\) with acid (\(\mathrm{HCO_{3}^{-} + H^{+} \rightarrow CO_{2} + H_{2}O}\)), and both contain sodium.

questions.q: A solution may contain carbonate, sulfate and chloride ions. A student wants to test for all three, one after another, on the same sample. Which sequence works?

options.A: Add dilute nitric acid until fizzing stops, then barium nitrate solution, then silver nitrate solution.
options.B: Add dilute hydrochloric acid until fizzing stops, then barium chloride solution, then silver nitrate solution.
options.C: Add silver nitrate solution first, then barium nitrate solution, then dilute nitric acid.
options.D: Add dilute sulfuric acid until fizzing stops, then barium nitrate solution, then silver nitrate solution.

questions.solution: Test for carbonate first with an acid that adds no ion being tested for: nitric acid. The acid also removes carbonate before the barium test. Then barium nitrate (not chloride) tests for sulfate, and silver nitrate tests for chloride last. (Hydrochloric acid or barium chloride would add chloride ions; sulfuric acid would add sulfate ions.)

questions.q: Which ionic equation represents a positive test for sulfate ions?
questions.solution: Barium ions form a white precipitate of insoluble barium sulfate: \(\mathrm{Ba^{2+}(aq) + SO_{4}^{2-}(aq) \rightarrow BaSO_{4}(s)}\). Barium carbonate is the false positive that the acid is added to prevent; barium chloride is soluble; and silver ions are used to test for halides (silver sulfate would be \(\mathrm{Ag_{2}SO_{4}}\)).
